etymology.text: From Middle High German kintheit, from Old High German kindheit (also kindesheit), equivalent to Kind (“child”) + -heit.

funFacts: -heit is the cousin of English -hood: Kindheit – childhood, Mannheit – manhood.
pitfalls: “When I was a child” is als ich ein Kind war or als ich klein war – not *in meinem Kind.
die Kindheit is feminine like every noun in -heit.
subtleties: The adverb of childhood memories is früher (in the past) or als Kind (as a child): Als Kind spielte ich oft im Garten.
Nouns in -heit, -keit, -ung are always feminine: die Kindheit, die Freiheit, die Wohnung.

etymology.text: Compound of Spiel (“game”) + Zeug (“stuff, gear”), or spielen (“to play”) + Zeug; Zeug is from Middle High German ziuc (“stuff, gear”) and is related to English toy.

funFacts: Zeug (stuff, gear) and English toy may be related: Wiktionary connects the two words.
pitfalls: In the singular Spielzeug often means “toys” as a mass: Er hat viel Spielzeug (lots of toys) – not *viele Spielzeug.
das Spielzeug is neuter like its last part, das Zeug.
subtleties: Spielzeuge (plural) counts kinds or pieces; viel Spielzeug (singular) is the usual way to talk about a pile of toys.
Figuratively: Er ist nur ihr Spielzeug (he is just her plaything).

etymology.text: From Middle High German spil, from Old High German spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“dance”).

funFacts: The Olympic Games are die Olympischen Spiele – plural, like in English.
pitfalls: ein Spiel spielen – the noun and the verb go together naturally; one does not *machen a game.
Genitive des Spiels or des Spieles, dative plural den Spielen.
subtleties: auf dem Spiel stehen = to be at stake; aufs Spiel setzen = to put at risk.
Spiel is also play in a machine (a loose part has Spiel – slack) and leeway (Spielraum).

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German spil(e)n, from Old High German spilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spilōn. Cognate with Bavarian spuin.

funFacts: Das spielt keine Rolle – literally “that plays no part” – is the everyday German for “it doesn’t matter”.
pitfalls: spielen is regular (weak): spielte, gespielt.
Sports and games need no article: Fußball spielen, Tennis spielen, Schach spielen.
subtleties: spielen also covers playing music and acting: Klavier spielen (play the piano), eine Rolle spielen (to play a part; also: to matter – Das spielt keine Rolle = it doesn’t matter).
A story spielt somewhere: Der Film spielt in Berlin (is set in Berlin).

funFacts: erwachsen (adult) is the participle of the verb erwachsen (to grow, to arise), a relative of wachsen.
pitfalls: The perfect takes sein: Ich bin in Berlin aufgewachsen – the usual way to tell where you grew up.
du wächst, er wächst: the stem ends in s, so du gets only -t after the umlaut (wächst).
subtleties: Separable and strong: wächst auf – wuchs auf – aufgewachsen.
wachsen alone is to grow (plants, children, a city): Das Kind wächst schnell.

etymology.text: From Middle High German erinnern, erinneren, from er- + innern, from Old High German innarōn (“to make someone perceive inwardly”), from innar (“inner”).

funFacts: The word hides inner: erinnern once meant “to make someone aware inwardly”.
pitfalls: To remember needs the reflexive pronoun and an: Ich erinnere mich an dich – not *Ich erinnere dich (that means “I remind you”).
Without sich, erinnern means to remind: Erinnere mich bitte an den Termin! (Please remind me of the appointment.)
an + accusative: Ich erinnere mich an den Tag (not *an dem Tag).
subtleties: er- is inseparable: no ge- in the participle (erinnert).
Regionally and colloquially also without sich and an: Ich erinnere das nicht (nonstandard) – the standard is Ich erinnere mich nicht daran.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vergëȥȥen, from Old High German firgëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan.

funFacts: English forget and German vergessen are twins: for-/ver- + get/gessen.
pitfalls: Infinitive and participle are the same: vergessen – ich habe vergessen (no ge-, because ver- is an inseparable prefix).
du vergisst, er vergisst, imperative vergiss! (e → i); ihr vergesst.
Präteritum with ß: vergaß, vergaßen.
subtleties: vergessen also means to leave something behind: Ich habe meinen Schirm im Bus vergessen.
Vergiss es! (forget it!) is an informal “never mind / no way”.

etymology.text: From Kind (“child”) + -er- + Garten (“garden”). Coined by the German educator Friedrich Fröbel in 1840 in the metaphorical sense of a place where children can grow in a natural way.

funFacts: English borrowed the word kindergarten from German together with Fröbel’s idea.
pitfalls: der Kindergarten is masculine like der Garten; plural die Kindergärten.
In German it is for children of about three to six, before school; it is not the first school year.
subtleties: in den Kindergarten gehen (to attend) – accusative of direction; im Kindergarten sein (to be there) – dative.
Colloquially Kindergarten also means childish squabbling: Das ist doch Kindergarten!

etymology.text: From Middle High German nāchbūr, nāchgebūr, from Old High German nāhgibūr, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwagabūrô (“neighbour”); equivalent to nah (“near”) + Bauer (“dweller”).

funFacts: Nachbar and English neighbour share their history: “near” + “dweller”, Bauer being the old word for a dweller before it meant farmer.
pitfalls: A weak noun: den Nachbarn, dem Nachbarn, des Nachbarn (colloquially des Nachbars, and den/dem Nachbar are heard, but the -n forms are the standard).
The plural is Nachbarn – the same as the singular forms after den/dem: context or the article decides.
subtleties: The woman is die Nachbarin; for a group of men and women the plural die Nachbarn is used (or Nachbarinnen und Nachbarn).
English neighbour has the same two parts: neigh- (near) + -bour (dweller, cf. German Bauer).

examples.text: In den Schulferien fuhren wir immer ans Meer.

examples.text: Die Schulferien beginnen im Juli.

the summer holidays (the longest school break)

etymology.text: Compound of Schule (“school”) + Ferien (“holidays”); Ferien is from Latin fēriae (15th century), with the Latin plural ending -ae replaced by German -en.

funFacts: Because the Länder stagger the summer holidays, German motorways see waves of holiday traffic from June to September.
pitfalls: Plural only: die Schulferien, in den Schulferien – there is no *die Schulferie.
Ferien are school (or university) holidays; adults at work have Urlaub: Ich habe im Juli Urlaub.
subtleties: In everyday speech Germans just say die Ferien; Schulferien is used when it must be clear (dates, calendars, news).
In Germany each federal state has its own school-holiday dates, so the summer holidays are staggered.

examples.text: Früher spielte ich jeden Tag im Garten.
examples.tr: I used to play in the garden every day.

examples.text: Früher bin ich oft mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule gefahren.

phrases.tr: In the past everything was better.
phrases.meaning: the nostalgic (often ironic) complaint about modern times

synonyms.nuance: back then, at that time – a definite moment in the past

etymology.text: Comparative of früh (“early”); as an adverb it has come to mean “formerly, in the past (often years ago, in contrast to nowadays)”.

funFacts: “Früher war alles besser” (everything used to be better) is the classic German grumble about the present.
pitfalls: German has no verb form for “used to”: früher (+ the Präteritum or the perfect) does the job – Früher wohnte ich in Berlin.
früher is also simply “earlier”: Komm bitte früher! (Please come earlier!) – the context decides.
subtleties: früher contrasts with heute (today, nowadays): Früher war alles anders – heute …
The adjective früher means former: mein früherer Lehrer (my former teacher).
